thread.title: Qualcomm steps into the nascent streaming gaming market

title: Qualcomm steps into the nascent streaming gaming market

organizations.name: bloomberg news ryan shrout analyst  qualcomm

text:
Qualcomm is partnering with a company that’s aiming to be the first streaming gaming provider for Android (and eventually Apple hardware) to succeed.
This shows that the hyper-scale server infrastructure expected to grow throughout the deployment period of the internet of things (IoT), and other services, is real. Start-up Hatch Entertainment, a spinoff of Finland’s Rovio Entertainment RVTTY, +0.00% is building a cloud-based streaming gaming service for mobile devices and will use San Diego-based Qualcomm’s QCOM, -2.17% Centriq 2400 server chips as the data-center heart of its platform. Rovio is best known for creating the popular “Angry Bids” game.
Qualcomm’s potential for revenue growth as the primary technology provider for Hatch is substantial. Last year’s revenue for smartphone gaming was $46 billion, and in 2018 it’s projected to be $57 billion . Separately, advertising revenue for mobile gaming was an additional $39 billion last year. 
Streaming games don’t require downloads or installation on consumers’ smartphones. Bandwidth requirements for the cellular carriers are half that of streaming video, a unique trait for the Hatch and Qualcomm design, which uses capabilities of Qualcomm’s server processor and local hardware on smartphone chips simultaneously. Staking a claim to this market segment could mean big growth for Qualcomm’s budding server unit.
Read: Broadcom is ‘evaluating its options’ for Qualcomm takeover after revised NXP bid 
For all its talk and technical prowess, Qualcomm needs customers and proof points to validate the cost and investment by management in this highly competitive space. Intel dominates the enterprise market with up to 99% market share, with fellow x86-architecture competitor AMD AMD, +3.09% releasing competitive processors last year for the first time in nearly a decade. Other Arm-based designs, including ones from Cavium CAVM, +1.70% Applied Micro Circuits and newcomer Ampere, led by an ex-Intel INTC, +2.41% president, have struggled to gain solid footing. Qualcomm has a strong brand in the consumer mobile chip and infrastructure markets but moving in on space dominated by Intel takes additional effort.
Hatch developers tell me that by using Qualcomm chips in the cloud, it can take advantage of architectural similarities between that processor and the ones that exist in smartphones from the Google GOOG, +1.32% Android and Apple AAPL, +0.96% iPhone ecosystem. The cloud-based games will run logic on the Qualcomm Centriq-based chips and then send specific instructions on what and how to render the graphics on the smartphone itself. This splits the processing between the cloud and local device, improving the gaming experience over previous streaming gaming. 
Hatch views the benefits of an Arm-based design like Qualcomm’s as key, with no need to convert games from their native Arm-based code that was developed for smartphones. This conversion would be required using Intel or AMD servers, and would mean a reduction in performance. Using Qualcomm Centriq 2400 chips saves processing time and power, making the service more scalable and less expensive to operate.
For Intel and AMD, both of which are fully entrenched in the traditional server space with x86 processors, this is a warning sign of a potential shift in the landscape of cloud services. As the available options of Arm-based servers continues to increase, developers will find more ways to use their capabilities for unique integrations, including what Hatch is showing. 
Other workloads typically run in the cloud that could shift to Qualcomm Centriq 2400 or competing designs include web hosting and long-term cold storage (hard drives that are accessed infrequently) that companies like Facebook FB, -0.07% and Google use to store the massive amounts of data uploaded by users every day.
The Qualcomm and Hatch announcement is only a single step in what must be a long journey for the chip giant to prove that it can attack the competitive and Intel-dominated server space. At a time when Qualcomm must substantiate the value of its adjacent product offerings due to the hostile takeover actions of Broadcom AVGO, +2.55% it must continue to bring in new, larger and more meaningful customers. 
Ryan Shrout is the founder and lead analyst at Shrout Research , and the owner of PC Perspective . Follow him on Twitter @ryanshrout .
